newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German industry output picks up in November.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German industry output picks up in November.

text.p: German industrial output picked up in November to show a rise of 1.6 percent against October, when a fall in output was revised down to 0.7 percent, the Economics Ministry said on Friday.
November industry output was up 1.3 percent on a year earlier after a 0.9 percent gain in October, the data, which are preliminary, showed.

The gain in the seasonally-adjusted output figures topped market expectations and snapped a two-month sequence of falling production which had started to worry economists predicting steady economic recovery.

They said that the November figure put Germany on course to show modest overall economic growth of around 1.5 percent for 1996, in line with government forecasts, but they warned that the latest cold spell could knock output back again.
"The production rise was to be expected given the rise in orders in October. It doesn't change our forecast that German GDP rose 1.5 percent in 1996," said Uwe Angenendt at BHF-Bank.
After solid gains in the second and third quarters, Angenendt said fourth quarter GDP would be stagnant or slightly higher.

But the economy is likely to stagnate in the first quarter of the new year due to the chill which has swept Germany, a hike in pension contributions which has just taken effect and the scrapping of some tax breaks in east Germany, he said.

Economists said that with consumer demand weak and the economy still largely being carried by export growth, the overall picture was still subdued and there was no inflationary pressure likely to cause concern at the Bundesbank.

"Growth in the fourth quarter will be flat at best and there may even be a small contraction. If we are looking at any growth in the consumer side we can forget about it. The economy will remain weak," Rob Hayward at Bank of America told Reuters Financial Television.
The industrial output data for November showed broad gains in manufacturing, with consumer durables leading with a gain of 4.2 percent. Construction activity was down by two percent.

German industrial production data are notoriously volatile and often subject to heavy revisions, and a broader comparison of the latest two months with August and September showed output unchanged overall.

West German industrial output was up two percent on October, and 2.1 percent higher than a year earlier. The tiny east German production sector saw output fall by 0.3 percent month-on-month and rise by 0.1 percent over a year earlier.
